lessons.title: 1 · Measurements: a number needs a method
lessons.goal: Calculate a mean and a range, distinguish consistency from accuracy, and investigate an unexpected reading without hiding it.
lessons.materials: Paper, pencil and optional calculator. All records below are invented for reasoning practice; they are not findings about real people or products. Work from the supplied records; no experiment or internet connection is required.
paragraphs:
BEFORE YOU CALCULATE
Two people write 10 on their cards. Did they measure the same thing? You cannot tell without the object, unit and method. Try naming three pieces of information you would need to repeat a length measurement.

BUILD THE IDEA
An observation records what was read or seen. An interpretation explains what it may mean. 'The ruler reading was 10.2 cm' is an observation. 'The card stretched' is a proposed explanation that needs more evidence. Write the object, unit, start/end rule and any unusual conditions with the reading.

WORKED EXAMPLE · MEAN AND RANGE
Three invented readings of another card are 8.0, 8.2 and 8.1 cm. The mean shares the total equally: (8.0 + 8.2 + 8.1) ÷ 3 = 24.3 ÷ 3 = 8.1 cm. The range describes the span: greatest − least = 8.2 − 8.0 = 0.2 cm. The mean has the original unit. It is not the total, and the range is not the number of readings.

WHAT REPEATING CAN AND CANNOT TELL YOU
Close repeated readings show consistency under those conditions. They do not establish closeness to a trusted reference: the same ruler or start error can affect every reading. Averaging can summarize a set; it does not automatically remove a shared error. A range of 0.2 cm describes these readings, not a guarantee that the true length lies within a particular interval.

WORKED REVISION · KEEP THE SURPRISE
Weak note: 'One reading was different, so I deleted it.' Better note: 'I kept all readings, marked the unusual one, checked the original record and the ruler alignment, and repeated the measurement with the same stated method.' If an actual transcription error is established, preserve the original and record the correction and reason. Do not remove a value merely because it is inconvenient.

READ THE CHART
Each bar below begins at zero and has its reading printed beside it. Similar bar lengths represent similar numbers. Use the labels for the exact values; do not estimate small differences from pixels. The chart summarizes the three original readings in M2, before the later reading in M4.

PRACTICE, THEN TRANSFER
Use M1–M4 for the new card. Enter a number without units; the unit is shown by the question. Explain your calculation. Then write a repeatable method and a response to the unexpected reading. Tomorrow, explain why three identical readings could still all share an error, using a different object.

PRACTICE RECORD
CARD LENGTH LOG — FICTIONAL PRACTICE DATA
[M1] Object: one rectangular paper card. The same person used the same ruler in one session. Each reading was recorded to the nearest 0.1 cm, with the start edge aligned to the zero mark.
[M2] Original readings: trial 1 = 10.0 cm; trial 2 = 10.2 cm; trial 3 = 10.1 cm.
[M3] The ruler has not been compared with a trusted reference. There is no independent reference length for the card in this record.
[M4] A later fourth reading is 10.9 cm. Its method was not written down. Keep it separate from the three original readings when answering questions that explicitly ask about M2.

questions.prompt: Using only the three original readings in M2, what is their mean?
questions.explanation: Add 10.0 + 10.2 + 10.1 = 30.3 cm, then divide by the three readings: 30.3 ÷ 3 = 10.1 cm. It is between the smallest and largest readings. M4 is excluded here because the question explicitly defines the set as M2, not because a surprising value may be discarded.
hints: Find the total for M2 only, then count its readings.
Share 30.3 equally among three readings.
mistakes: That is the total. A mean shares the total among the readings.
M2 contains three readings, not four. Match the count to the values included.

lessons.title: 2 · Fair comparisons: what actually changed?
lessons.goal: Separate an observed difference from its cause, calculate mean times, and design a comparison that addresses a competing explanation.
lessons.materials: Paper, pencil and optional calculator. All records below are invented for reasoning practice; they are not findings about real people or products. Work from the supplied records; no experiment or internet connection is required.
paragraphs:
START WITH A RIVAL EXPLANATION
Someone sorts cards faster after receiving new labels. Before crediting the labels, list another thing that might have changed: practice, the card set, distractions, timing rules or help. An observed difference is the starting point for inquiry, not the end.

NAME THE VARIABLES
A variable is something that can differ. Here the proposed change is the label design. The measured outcome is elapsed sorting time in seconds. Conditions such as card set, instructions and prior practice can also affect time. If labels and practice change together, the recorded difference alone cannot separate their effects; that is a confounded comparison.

WORKED EXAMPLE · COMPARE SUMMARIES
In a separate invented test, times for design P are 18, 20 and 22 seconds; for Q they are 14, 16 and 18. The means are 60 ÷ 3 = 20 and 48 ÷ 3 = 16 seconds. Q's mean is 4 seconds lower in those records. The means summarize the data; they do not show that Q wins every trial or that labels alone caused the difference.

IMPROVE THE COMPARISON
Use the same card set, instructions, room conditions and timing rule. Give the same practice rule for each design. Use both starting orders: some sessions X then Y, others Y then X, with a planned order rule rather than choosing the order after seeing results. Record all trials and deviations. This addresses order effects better than always trying Y second, but small tests still have limits.

READ THE CHART
The bars summarize the new records in C2. Lower means mean less time, not automatically better work. Accuracy was not recorded. A faster sort with more errors could be less useful, so a follow-up should define and record an accuracy measure too.

WORKED REVISION
Weak: 'Y is best because it was faster.' Better: 'Y had a lower mean time in these sessions, but Y followed extra practice. We need a comparison that balances order and measures errors before deciding whether the label design helped.' Notice how the revision preserves the observed difference and changes the explanation.

TRANSFER
In Practice, calculate the actual means and identify what the design cannot separate. Then plan a repeat with enough detail for someone to audit the method. Try applying the same questions to two sets of written instructions: what changed, what was measured, and what else could explain it?

PRACTICE RECORD
CARD SORTING PILOT — FICTIONAL PRACTICE DATA
[C1] One person sorted the same 20 cards. All three X-label trials happened first. Then the person received extra practice and completed all three Y-label trials. Timing started at the first card pickup and ended when all cards were placed.
[C2] X times: 12, 14, 16 seconds. Y times: 8, 10, 12 seconds. All six recorded trials are shown.
[C3] No count of sorting errors was recorded. There were no other participants or sessions.
[C4] Proposed follow-up: compare the label designs while recording both elapsed time and the number of cards placed correctly.

questions.prompt: What is the mean X-label time in C2?
questions.explanation: X totals 12 + 14 + 16 = 42 seconds across three trials. 42 ÷ 3 = 14 seconds. This is a mean time for X in this pilot, not for all six trials or all future users.

mistakes: That is X's total time. Divide by the number of X trials to find the mean.

lessons.title: 3 · Samples: compare rates, then ask who is missing
lessons.goal: Compare proportions with unequal denominators, distinguish percentage points from counts, and identify limits of a self-selected sample.
lessons.materials: Paper, pencil and optional calculator. All records below are invented for reasoning practice; they are not findings about real people or products. Work from the supplied records; no experiment or internet connection is required.
paragraphs:
PREDICT BEFORE DIVIDING
Group A has 8 successful attempts and group B has 18. Is B more successful? You need the total attempts in each group. Counts answer 'how many'; a proportion compares the count with its own total. Never quietly switch those totals.

BUILD THE IDEA · COUNT, FRACTION, PERCENT
A proportion is selected count ÷ total count. For 6 out of 8, this is 6/8 = 3/4 = 0.75. A percent expresses that amount per hundred: 75%. For 9 out of 12, 9/12 is also 3/4. Nine is a larger count, but these two proportions are equal.

WORKED EXAMPLE · PERCENTAGE POINTS
Compare 75% with 50%. Their difference is 25 percentage points: 75 − 50 = 25. A relative percent increase asks a different question and needs a baseline: 25 ÷ 50 × 100 = 50% relative increase. In this lesson, questions that say 'percentage points' ask for simple subtraction of the percentages, not a relative change.

ASK WHO THE SAMPLE REPRESENTS
A sample is a subset of the people or cases of interest. Volunteers can differ from nonvolunteers. If people choose which instruction version to try, the groups may differ in experience or other ways before the task begins. Dividing by each group size gives a fair numerical rate comparison, but it does not remove selection bias or establish cause.

READ THE CHART
The two bars show the percentages from S2 on a common 0–100% axis. Labels name both groups. The chart must be read with the denominators: 10 people tried one version and 30 tried the other. It summarizes these volunteers, not all potential users.

WORKED REVISION
Weak: 'The larger success count proves the better instructions.' Better: 'Compare success proportions using each group's own total, then describe who chose each version and who was absent. A higher observed proportion can justify a better-planned follow-up; it does not by itself identify what caused the difference.'

TRANSFER
Answer the rate questions, identify a more useful sampling plan, then rewrite an overclaim. For the final task, use different numbers to show why a larger success count can still correspond to the same proportion. Explain the denominator, not just the division.

PRACTICE RECORD
INSTRUCTION CARD TRIAL — FICTIONAL PRACTICE DATA
[S1] Forty volunteers at a single afternoon club chose which instruction card to try. Ten chose large print; thirty chose standard print. Each person attempted the same paper sorting task once. Success meant placing every card correctly; no completion time was recorded.
[S2] Large print: 8 successes out of 10 attempts. Standard print: 18 successes out of 30 attempts. All attempts are included.
[S3] Previous experience and reasons for choosing a version were not recorded. People who could not attend that afternoon were not included.
[S4] The intended users include morning and evening groups as well as this afternoon club. A follow-up could invite people across those groups and assign versions by chance instead of by preference.

questions.prompt: What fraction of large-print attempts succeeded in S2? Enter an exact fraction or decimal, not a percent.
questions.explanation: Use the large-print denominator: 8 ÷ 10 = 8/10 = 4/5 = 0.8. Eight is the success count; 40 is the total across both groups and is not the denominator for the large-print success rate.
hints: Match the numerator and denominator to the same version.
Eight successes out of ten attempts can be simplified by dividing both counts by two.
mistakes: Forty combines both groups. The question asks for the fraction within the ten large-print attempts.
Eighty is the percentage number. Here enter the fraction 8/10 or an equivalent exact decimal.

questions.explanation: Broader invitations address the omitted time groups; chance assignment addresses preference-based grouping. Record participation and nonresponse because invitations do not guarantee a representative sample. Keep the task and success rule common. These steps improve the design, without guaranteeing a particular outcome.
hints: There are two issues: who could attend, and how versions were chosen.
Look for a plan addressing both, while retaining unsuccessful attempts.
mistakes: B
More people from the same narrow group do not automatically address missing users or self-selection.
C

lessons.title: 4 · Evidence report: make a claim you can defend
lessons.goal: Combine calculations, design details and missing records into a qualified claim and a concrete next investigation.
lessons.materials: Paper, pencil and optional calculator. All records below are invented for reasoning practice; they are not findings about real people or products. Work from the supplied records; no experiment or internet connection is required.
paragraphs:
THE CHALLENGE
A club wants to decide whether to develop picture-supported instructions. Your job is to write a useful report from the supplied pilot. A useful report includes both the evidence in favor and the reasons for uncertainty. It neither promises a result the records cannot show nor discards the observations because the test is imperfect.

READ THE METHOD BEFORE THE TOTALS
Identify the intended change, who took part, the assignment method, the scoring rule and missing records. Assignment by chance is a way to reduce systematic group differences; it cannot make small groups identical or recover missing outcomes. A score is meaningful only with its denominator and rule.

WORKED EXAMPLE · KEEP THE DENOMINATOR VISIBLE
In a separate invented exercise, four returned sheets score 6, 7, 8 and 7 correct out of 10 each. The total is 28 correct out of 40 recorded items, or 70%. That is an item-level percentage. It is not the percentage of people who achieved a perfect score, and it is not a score for sheets that were never returned.

SEPARATE THE LAYERS
Observation: a recorded score or total. Summary: a mean, proportion or difference computed from those records. Interpretation: what the comparison suggests under the method used. Decision: what to do next, given the purpose and uncertainty. Labeling these layers helps you catch a jump from one small pilot to a universal claim.

WORKED REVISION · A USEFUL LIMIT
Weak: 'Missing data means we learned nothing.' Better: 'The returned sheets favor one version under this scoring rule, but we do not know whether the missing sheets would change the comparison. Follow up on missing outcomes and repeat with a larger, more varied group before generalizing.' Do not code an unreturned sheet as all wrong or all right unless a scoring rule established in advance explicitly calls for it.

READ THE CHART
The bars show the percentage of correctly placed cards among the returned sheets in R3, using 50 recorded card placements per version. They do not show every invited participant's score. Check the numbers against the log and keep the missing records in your explanation.

WRITE, AUDIT, REVISE
After the short checks, write a 4–6 sentence report: question and method, computed result, what it suggests, two limits, and a next step. Underline every factual claim and point to its supporting record. Circle claims that would need new evidence. Then compare with the worked report and revise in your own words.

PRACTICE RECORD
PICTURE INSTRUCTIONS PILOT — FICTIONAL PRACTICE DATA
[R1] Fourteen afternoon-club volunteers were assigned by drawing lots: seven to text-only instructions (A), seven to the same text plus pictures (B). Each was given the same ten-card sorting task, the same time allowance and the same definition of a correct placement.
[R2] Five sheets were returned in each group. Two from A and two from B were not returned; their scores and reasons for nonreturn are unknown. Score only the returned sheets in the calculations below.
[R3] Correct placements, each out of 10: A = 7, 8, 8, 9, 8; B = 9, 9, 10, 9, 8.
[R4] No task-completion times, later retention scores or morning/evening-user results were collected.
[R5] Proposed decision: whether the pilot justifies further development and a better documented follow-up, not whether pictures are proven best for every user.

questions.prompt: How many correct card placements are recorded on the five returned B sheets in R3?
questions.explanation: Add 9 + 9 + 10 + 9 + 8 = 45 correct placements. This is a total, not the mean score of 9 per returned sheet. The two missing sheets have unknown outcomes and are not added as zeroes.
hints: Use every B value exactly once.
Add the five returned scores; do not supply invented scores for the missing sheets.
mistakes: Nine is the mean per returned B sheet. This question asks for the total across the five sheets.
Fifty is the maximum possible on the five returned sheets, not the number actually correct.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion best matches R1–R5?
choices: A
Pictures are proven to improve every user's score and speed.
B
The missing sheets prove the pictures did not help.
C
Returned B sheets had 90% correct placements versus A's 80%; that supports further study, with limits from missing records and the small sample.
questions.explanation: A totals 40/50 = 80%, and B totals 45/50 = 90% among returned sheets. The pilot favors B on this immediate scoring measure. Missing scores and a small, narrow volunteer group limit interpretation. No speed or retention effect was measured; the missing sheets do not prove either success or failure.
hints: Compute A's total and check which outcomes R4 says were not collected.
A defensible claim can report the difference and still state its limits.
mistakes: A
R4 has no timing data, and this small volunteer sample cannot establish results for every user.
B
Unknown scores are unknown. They do not establish that one design helped or failed.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the missing sheets is justified by R2?
choices: A
The same number is missing in each group, so missing data cannot change the comparison.
B
Their outcomes are unknown; record the missingness and seek the scores or reasons without inventing them.
C
Count all missing sheets as perfect because they were probably easy.
questions.explanation: Equal counts of missing sheets do not imply equal missing scores or reasons. Preserve what is known and unknown, try to recover the records appropriately, and explain the limit if recovery is impossible. Neither perfect nor zero scores are established by R2.
hints: Does equal missing count tell you the missing scores?
Separate absence of a record from evidence about performance.
mistakes: A
Two unknown scores per group could differ. Equal missing counts do not guarantee equal effects on the comparison.

questions.prompt: Write a 4–6 sentence report for the club. Include method, both rates, a qualified interpretation, at least two limitations and a useful next step.
questions.explanation: Audit for: (1) assignment by lots and a common task, (2) returned-sheet A = 40/50 = 80%, B = 45/50 = 90%, (3) a ten-percentage-point descriptive difference, (4) missing sheets plus narrow sample or unmeasured outcomes, (5) a next action tied to a limit. Example: 'Fourteen volunteers were assigned by lots to text-only or picture-supported instructions for the same sorting task. Among five returned sheets per group, A had 40/50 correct placements (80%) and B 45/50 (90%). This favors developing and testing B further on this immediate task. Two sheets per group are missing, and the afternoon sample says little about other users or later retention. Record reasons for nonreturn where available and repeat with a broader group and a planned way to collect every outcome.' Wording can differ. A numerical match does not automatically validate the report.
hints: Write one sentence for the method and one for the returned-sheet result before interpreting it.
For every limitation, ask what information or procedure would address it.

questions.explanation: Compare for a testable question and an auditable plan. Example: 'Do pictures increase correct placements for morning and evening volunteers on the same ten-card task?
